result: Anti-Endos phosphatase activity is present during M phase in Xenopus egg extracts, while anti-CDKS (PP2A-B55) activity is blocked during M phase and induced upon Ca2+ treatment triggering M phase exit.
evaluation: Claims C13 and C14 are directly demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2A showing differential regulation of these two activities during the cell cycle. This establishes the key observation that anti-Endos remains active when PP2A-B55 activity toward CDK substrates is suppressed.

result: The predominant anti-Endos activity (70-90% of total) is sensitive to okadaic acid, calyculin A, and fostriecin, but resistant to cyclosporin A, indicating it belongs to the PP2A/PP4/PP6 subfamily of PPP phosphatases.
evaluation: Claims C15-C18 are supported by comprehensive inhibitor sensitivity data across multiple cell types (Figure 2B-C and supplements). The fostriecin sensitivity specifically narrows candidates to PP2A/PP4/PP6, while okadaic acid and calyculin A sensitivity confirms PPP family membership.

result: Anti-Endos activity differs from anti-CDKS activity in being 6-10 fold more resistant to tautomycetin, substantially resistant to phosphomimetic Endos S68D, and minimally affected by extract dilution.
evaluation: Claims C19-C21 are directly demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2D-F and supplements. These differential properties initially suggested anti-Endos might be a different enzyme than PP2A-B55, but are later explained by the extreme differences in Km values between substrates.

result: RNAi/siRNA depletion of PP2A catalytic or A subunits removes 70-75% of anti-Endos activity, while depletion of PP1, PP4, PP5, or PP6 has minimal or no effect on anti-Endos levels.
evaluation: Claims C22-C27 are supported by RNAi experiments in Drosophila S2 cells (Figure 3) and siRNA/knockout experiments in mammalian cells (Figure 3 supplements). The specificity for PP2A components strongly implicates a PP2A-containing enzyme as the major anti-Endos phosphatase.

result: Drosophila larvae homozygous for mutations in twins (encoding the sole B55 regulatory subunit) lack both anti-CDKS and anti-Endos activities, while activity against Histone H1v1.0 is unaffected and PP2A-A and PP2A-C protein levels remain normal.
evaluation: Claims C28-C30 are directly demonstrated by phosphatase assays and Western blots from twins mutant larvae (Figure 4). This genetic evidence specifically identifies the B55 regulatory subunit as essential for anti-Endos activity, strongly supporting PP2A-B55 as the enzyme. Statistical significance is reported (p<10^-20).

result: Anti-Endos and anti-CDKS activities co-purify during Mono-Q chromatography and peak in fractions containing all three PP2A-B55 subunits (A, B55, C), while separating from PP4, PP5, PP6, and other PP2A regulatory subunits.
evaluation: Claims C31-C33 are supported by fractionation data in Figure 5 showing co-elution of both activities with PP2A-B55 components. This biochemical purification provides strong evidence that a single enzyme (PP2A-B55) is responsible for both activities.

result: Purified recombinant PP2A-B55 heterotrimers (B55α and B55δ isoforms) efficiently dephosphorylate both pEndos and pCDKS substrates with similar fostriecin sensitivity, while PP2A-B56β heterotrimers and PP2A A-C dimers show no activity; anti-Endos activity is less sensitive to tautomycetin and phosphomimetic Endos than anti-CDKS activity.
evaluation: Claims C34-C38 are supported by experiments with purified enzymes (Figure 6). The demonstration that purified PP2A-B55 has both activities with properties matching those in extracts provides definitive evidence that PP2A-B55 is the anti-Endos enzyme. The differential inhibitor sensitivities are consistent with the Km differences discovered later.

result: The kcat for PP2A-B55 dephosphorylation of pEndos is 2-3 orders of magnitude slower than for CDK-phosphorylated substrates, while the Km is 4-5 orders of magnitude lower.
evaluation: Claims C4 and C5 are supported by rigorous kinetic measurements presented in Table 1 and Figure 7, using both traditional Michaelis-Menten analysis accounting for tight binding and an okadaic acid competition method. Multiple independent experiments with different enzyme preparations are reported. The extreme differences in kinetic parameters are the foundation of the 'inhibition by unfair competition' model.

result: pEndos interacts with the active site of PP2A-B55 and does not inhibit its own dephosphorylation at high concentrations through allosteric mechanisms.
evaluation: Claim C45 is supported by Figure 7B showing constant reaction rate over a 20-fold pEndos concentration range. Claim C46 is supported by evidence that pEndos is dephosphorylated by PP2A-B55 and competes with okadaic acid (known active site inhibitor). These findings support the competitive inhibition model rather than allosteric regulation.

result: Thiophosphorylated Endos inhibits PP2A-B55 with IC50 of 197±14 pM (only ~2-fold higher than okadaic acid), while nonphosphorylated Endos has IC50 of 566±65 nM, representing a ~3000-fold increase in binding affinity upon phosphorylation.
evaluation: Claims C47-C50 are supported by dose-response experiments in Figure 8A with technical replicates (n=3). The measurements demonstrate the extremely tight binding of phosphorylated Endos to PP2A-B55, comparable to the well-characterized inhibitor okadaic acid, supporting the inhibition by unfair competition mechanism.

result: PP2A-B55 can auto-reactivate by dephosphorylating pEndos, as demonstrated by experiments showing PP2A-B55 cannot recognize pCDKS substrate until the majority of pEndos is dephosphorylated, with a ~35 min delay in pCDKS dephosphorylation when pEndos is present.
evaluation: Claims C51-C53 are supported by in vitro competition experiments (Figure 8A-B) that directly test the auto-reactivation mechanism. The time-course data showing delayed pCDKS dephosphorylation in the presence of pEndos provides strong evidence for the proposed mechanism. The experiments include technical replicates (n=3) with error bars.

result: The intracellular concentration of PP2A B55 is estimated at 100-250 nM and Endos at 500 nM-1 μM (ratio ~5:1), consistent with estimates from other laboratories and mass spectrometry studies.
evaluation: Claims C54-C56 are supported by Western blot quantitation (Figure 2 supplement 6) and comparison with published mass spectrometry data. The 5:1 molar excess of Endos over PP2A-B55 is critical for the inhibition mechanism to function as proposed. The estimates are consistent with multiple independent data sources.

result: Mathematical modeling predicts that under physiological conditions, half of PP2A-B55 is released from pEndos sequestration within 74 seconds after Gwl inactivation, and that pEndos dephosphorylation by PP2A-B55 is an absolute requirement for rapid M phase exit; if pEndos were only an inhibitor and not a substrate, many hours would be required for exit.
evaluation: Claims C58-C60 are supported by mathematical modeling (Figure 10) using experimentally determined kinetic parameters. The modeling demonstrates the biological plausibility of the mechanism and explains why PP2A-B55 must dephosphorylate pEndos for timely M phase exit. The calculations are clearly described in Materials and Methods.

result: A phosphatase other than PP2A-B55 must inactivate Gwl during M phase exit, as purified PP2A-B55 is inefficient at inactivating Gwl in vitro, and active Gwl added to interphase extracts is rapidly inactivated in an okadaic acid-insensitive manner.
evaluation: Claims C61-C63 are based on preliminary unpublished data and logical inference. While the reasoning is sound (PP2A-B55 cannot inactivate Gwl if it's sequestered by pEndos), the experimental evidence is not shown. This represents an important gap requiring future investigation.

result: Fcp1 is not a major anti-Endos phosphatase: RNAi depletion of >90% Fcp1 has no effect on anti-Endos activity, purified Fcp1 has <1/1000th the efficiency of PP2A-B55, cells contain >10-fold more PP2A-B55 than Fcp1, Fcp1 does not co-fractionate with anti-Endos activity, and Fcp1 is completely resistant to okadaic acid.
evaluation: Claims C64-C68 and C70 are supported by multiple lines of evidence (Figure 11) including RNAi, enzyme kinetics, protein abundance estimates, chromatography, and inhibitor sensitivity. This comprehensive analysis effectively refutes the competing hypothesis that Fcp1 is the anti-Endos phosphatase, addressing a conflicting publication.

result: Background on M phase regulation: Entry into M phase requires phosphorylation of thousands of sites by CDKs including MPF; PP2A-B55 removes these phosphorylations at M phase exit; MPF activates Gwl which phosphorylates Endos; pEndos inhibits PP2A-B55; this pathway is critical for M phase entry and maintenance.
evaluation: Claims C1-C2 and C6-C12 represent established background knowledge supported by multiple citations to prior work. These claims provide essential context for understanding the current study but are not novel findings of this manuscript.

result: M phase exit is completed within less than 5 minutes in Xenopus cycling extracts.
evaluation: Claim C57 is supported by citations to prior work and provides important context for evaluating whether the proposed mechanism is kinetically feasible for the observed timing of M phase exit.

result: Purified PP1 is more sensitive to tautomycetin than purified PP2A A-C dimer when tested with myelin basic protein substrate.
evaluation: Claim C69 is supported by experimental data (Figure 2 supplement 3A) and is consistent with prior literature. This control experiment validates the expected differential sensitivity of PP1 vs PP2A to tautomycetin.
